summary: Describes the architecture of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). It extends label switching beyond packet routers to optical and transmission equipment such as DWDM systems and cross-connects, so the network can set up paths dynamically and recover from failures.

plainLanguage.summary: It takes the idea of reserving a route through a network and applies it to light beams and cables, not just to packets, with smart ways to switch to a backup road.

questions: what is lmp link management protocol
subtitle: How MPLS-style label switching is stretched to control time slots, wavelengths and whole fibers, not just packets.

tldr.problem: MPLS assumed equipment that can read packet or cell headers. Optical and transmission gear switches on time slots, wavelengths or physical ports, and it can have hundreds of parallel links between two nodes.
tldr.mechanism: GMPLS reuses the IP routing and MPLS-TE signaling model, adds a generalized label and label request, and adds unnumbered links, link bundling, forwarding adjacencies and the Link Management Protocol (LMP) to cope with scale and with separate control and data planes.
tldr.outcome: It describes one control plane for five interface classes, with signaling (RSVP-TE or CR-LDP), routing (OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE), link management, and protection and restoration. The unit metadata lists RFC 6002 as updating it.

facts.label: Generic bandwidth encoding
facts.value: 32-bit IEEE floating point, bytes per second

today: RFC 3945 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 6002 as updating it. No RFC is listed as obsoleting it.

sections.title: Five Classes of Switching Interface
sections.content:
Traditional MPLS assumes label switching routers (LSRs) that recognize packet or cell boundaries. GMPLS extends this to interfaces that switch on time slots, wavelengths or physical ports. The RFC sorts interfaces into five classes: PSC (packet switch capable), L2SC (layer-2 switch capable, such as Ethernet or ATM), TDM (time-division multiplex capable, such as SONET/SDH), LSC (lambda switch capable, switching by wavelength) and FSC (fiber-switch capable, switching by physical position).

A circuit can be established only between, or through, interfaces of the same type. Whatever each technology calls its circuit (SDH circuit, optical trail, light-path), GMPLS calls them all a Label Switched Path (LSP).

LSPs can nest to form a forwarding hierarchy. From the top, FSC contains LSC, which contains TDM, which contains L2SC, which contains PSC. A packet LSP can ride inside a layer-2 LSP, inside a TDM LSP, inside a wavelength LSP, inside a fiber LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of nesting boxes. A small parcel goes in a box, that box goes in a bigger box, and so on, up to a whole cable. Each size of box is a different kind of switching, and each box can only be handed to a worker who handles that size.

sections.title: Extending the MPLS Control Plane
sections.content:
The architecture separates the control plane from the forwarding plane, and splits the control plane into a signaling plane and a routing plane. It is a generalization of the MPLS architecture in RFC 3031, built on the traffic engineering extensions to MPLS described in RFC 2702. It supports overlay, augmented and peer (integrated) models and does not dictate how layers work together.

For signaling, GMPLS extends both RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and CR-LDP (RFC 3212) and does not say which must be used. For routing, it extends OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE. Extensions for inter-domain routing such as BGP are left for further study. Only one new protocol is required, the Link Management Protocol (LMP).

Key differences from MPLS-TE include labels that encode a time slot, wavelength or physical position, a wider range of payloads (SONET/SDH, G.709, Ethernet), bi-directional LSPs, label suggestion and restriction by the upstream node, selection of the egress port, and rapid failure notification with RSVP-TE. Bandwidth on TDM, LSC and FSC links can be allocated only in discrete units, and such links are expected to have far fewer labels than PSC or L2SC links.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a whole new road system, the designers kept the existing traffic rules and added a few new signs for roads made of light and time slots.

sections.title: Routing, Addressing and Scaling
sections.content:
GMPLS keeps the IP addressing and routing model: IPv4 or IPv6 addresses identify any interface, and link-state protocols discover topology. Routes for non-packet circuits are found with a constrained shortest path first (CSPF) algorithm. A TE link is a logical link with traffic engineering properties. It need not match one physical link or an IGP adjacency.

With DWDM, two nodes can be joined by hundreds of parallel links, which is impractical to number, advertise and keep as separate adjacencies. Two optional mechanisms help:

  • Unnumbered links have no IP address. Each end picks a local identifier and the two ends exchange them, by configuration, by LMP, by RSVP-TE or CR-LDP, or by IS-IS or OSPF extensions.
  • Link bundling advertises several links as one bundled link made of component links. Component links must share the same link type, TE metric and set of resource classes, and admission control is applied per component link. A bundled link is alive when at least one component link is alive.

A route normally names the bundled link, and the upstream node chooses the component link. It tells the downstream node in one of three ways: implicitly by sending on a dedicated signaling channel, explicitly by a numbered interface ID (an IP address), or explicitly by an unnumbered interface ID (a 32-bit value).
sections.plainLanguage: If a road has hundreds of lanes, you do not want a separate signpost for each. Bundling tells everyone it is one wide road, and a lane is picked only when a car actually sets off.

sections.title: Link Management Protocol
sections.content:
In GMPLS the control channel does not have to use the same medium as the data links, so a healthy control channel says nothing about the health of the data links. LMP runs between data-plane adjacent nodes to manage this. Its procedures are control channel management and link property correlation, which are mandatory, and link connectivity verification and fault management, which are optional.

  • Control channel management: establishes and maintains control channels with a fast Hello protocol in a negotiation phase and a keep-alive phase. Messages must be IP encoded, and each direction of a control channel gets a 32-bit non-zero Control Channel Identifier.
  • Link property correlation: exchanges link summary messages to build bundles and to change parameters such as reservable bandwidth.
  • Link connectivity verification: sends Test messages in-band over the data links, which is the only LMP message sent on a data link, to check physical connectivity and swap link identifiers.
  • Fault management: a downstream node that sees a data-link failure notifies its upstream neighbor, which can then localize the fault and start protection or restoration.

LMP-WDM extends LMP for use between an optical cross-connect and a DWDM optical line system, giving all-optical switches better visibility into the health of a channel.
sections.plainLanguage: LMP is two neighbours on the phone checking that the wires between them go where they should, and telling each other quickly if one breaks.

sections.title: Generalized Signaling
sections.content:
Signaling follows the MPLS profile of downstream-on-demand label allocation with ingress-initiated ordered control, and normally uses explicit routing. The core specifications are RFC 3471 (functional description), RFC 3473 (RSVP-TE) and RFC 3472 (CR-LDP), with RFC 3946 for SONET/SDH. The RFC lists twelve building blocks. Only the generalized label request, the generalized label and the per-technology traffic parameters are mandatory.

To request an LSP, the ingress sends a Path or Label Request carrying a Generalized Label Request with three items: the LSP Encoding Type (the technology), the Switching Type to use on a link, and the Generalized PID (the payload). The downstream node answers with a Generalized Label, a time slot, wavelength or fiber position. Bandwidth for technologies without specific parameters is a 32-bit IEEE floating-point number in bytes per second.

Other features include waveband switching, a suggested label to cut setup time on slow optical hardware, and a Label Set that restricts the upstream node's choice, which helps where wavelength conversion is unavailable. Bi-directional LSPs are set up with one set of messages, signaled by an Upstream Label. If two requests collide, the node with the higher node ID wins. Link protection information, explicit labels in the explicit route, route recording and an Admin Status object (to suppress alarms while an LSP is being deleted) complete the set.
sections.plainLanguage: To book a path, the sender says what kind of signal it needs, and each step along the way answers with exactly which slot, colour or fiber it has set aside. Booking both directions at once saves a second trip.

sections.title: Forwarding Adjacencies and Adjacencies
sections.content:
A forwarding adjacency (FA) turns an LSP into a TE link advertised in IS-IS or OSPF, so other LSRs can use it in path computation and nest their own LSPs inside it. Intermediate nodes see only the outer LSP, which cuts the forwarding state and signaling they must keep. An FA inherits its TE attributes from the LSP that created it, and its bandwidth must be at least as big as that LSP. FAs are not expected to be used for IS-IS or OSPF peering between the ends.

Interface switching capability is advertised per interface. When an LSP must cross a region boundary it can trigger an FA in the layer below, cascading in the order L2SC, TDM, LSC, then FSC.

Routing and signaling adjacencies are separate ideas. A TE link can exist between two nodes with no routing adjacency, but nodes need a signaling adjacency to set up LSPs, and an IP path between them, which can run over control channels when the TE link cannot carry packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If many small trips go the same way, a big shuttle is booked once and the small trips ride inside it. The stops in between only need to know about the shuttle.

sections.title: Faults, Protection and Restoration
sections.content:
Two control plane faults are named: a control channel fault, where communication is lost between neighbours, and a nodal fault, where a node loses control state but keeps forwarding. Neither should disturb existing connections, so state must be resynchronized after recovery. RFC 3473 covers both cases and RFC 3479 covers control channel failure for LDP.

For data plane faults, recovery runs through fault detection, localization, notification, recovery and reversion. Protection sets up resources before failure and only switches afterwards. Examples are 1+1 and 1:N link protection and 1+1 LSP protection. Restoration signals after failure, either with re-provisioning or with pre-signaled bandwidth, with or without label pre-selection. Operators choose by robustness, recovery time and resource sharing. The RFC cites a SONET/SDH protection switching objective of 50 ms, not counting detection time.

Multi-layer networks risk a storm of notifications when a lower layer fails. The RFC asks that a single notification be emitted from the lower interface and that MIB modules provide ways to enable, disable and summarize notifications. It also recommends SNMP and standard MIB modules for management.
sections.plainLanguage: If a road breaks, you can have a spare road ready and switch instantly, or work out a detour after the break. The spare is faster but costs more; the detour is cheaper but slower.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because GMPLS LSPs can carry large volumes of data and use significant network resources, the control plane should include mechanisms that prevent or minimize attackers injecting or snooping on control traffic. The risk depends on the trust between nodes and on the control channel: an in-band channel over SONET/SDH overhead bytes is generally considered less vulnerable than one over an out-of-band IP network.

Where only authentication is needed, the authentication of the component protocols may be used. IPsec may provide authentication, confidentiality or both for a control channel. Control elements should also check requests against local authorization policy, using the verified identity of the requester. The RFC states that GMPLS itself introduces no new security considerations beyond those of MPLS-TE signaling, routing protocols and SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the controls can move huge amounts of traffic, only trusted voices should be allowed to give orders, and the messages should be checked and, if needed, locked.
